text:
The migration passed every staging run. Staging used a 40 GB snapshot seeded with synthetic rows. In production, the migration failed forty minutes in, because the real orders table held 1.2 billion rows and a decade of drift.

The migration was an ALTER TABLE that added a NOT NULL column with a default. On PostgreSQL 10, that forces a rewrite of the entire heap. The rewrite first waited behind long-running checkout transactions. It then requested an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and every write that arrived afterward had to wait for that lock to clear.

Requests piled up with nothing able to move, and connection pool exhaustion alerts paged on-call within ninety seconds. The engineers had assumed the default was metadata-only. That fast path arrived in PostgreSQL 11, not 10. The rollback runbook had never been rehearsed, and running it cost another twenty minutes.

Staging had misled the team by leaving things out. Teams now take three steps:

- They shadow-migrate against full-size clones.
- They set lock_timeout to 5 seconds to limit how long DDL can wait.
- They backfill in batches before tightening constraints.

Some people call this approach "expand, then squeeze."
